blocks.p: Year five. Tarren, S. Fifty-five by the calipers, and holding. Weight up two kilos, which the subject puts down to his wife’s cooking and his wife to his. Seizures since the last entry: three, each announced by oranges. Tongue bitten once. He has begun to hum while he works. Denies it.
The roof of the house across the yard leaked over the end of the table, and Lyda kept a tin cup under the place.
“When it needs a basin, I’ll have it seen to,” she said, the first time Sol offered to go up with a ladder. “It’s a cup leak. I know what it costs me.”

So on rain evenings the cup sang, a note that rose as it filled, and Sol, who had lived a century in a residence where rain was let into the gardens for twenty minutes at a time and never came indoors uninvited, listened for it as he had once listened for the bell of the evening office.

He was at the stove. He had learned to cook at fifty-three by the body’s count, from the baker’s wife, who said he had good hands and no sense. Tobin had brought a fish up from the pier, and Sol was doing something to it in a pan, and Lyda sat at the dry end of the table with the day’s manifests and a red pencil.
“Bishop’s minute,” she said, without looking up.

On the Thorne pier any delay at all had come to be called a bishop’s minute, because that was how long it took Sol to sign a manifest. He had done the counting for the line for three years, and his figures were never wrong. The trouble came at the bottom of the sheet. For most of his life he had signed with a thought, in the corner of his sight, as easily as blinking. Now his name came out of a pen at the end of his own arm, in the square stiff capitals Lucan called an engineer’s hand, and every time he reached the line his hand stopped by itself above it and waited. The loaders sat down on the bales. The masters waited at their ramps.
“Hollis stood at the Kestrel’s ramp most of an hour this morning,” Lyda said. “Eleven sheets.”
“Twelve.”
“Twelve.” She made a small red mark. “She asked me whether you were praying over them.”
He turned the fish. It stuck. “In a way.”
“What are you waiting for?”
He thought about it honestly, because she would know if he did not. “To be sure it’s reed.”
She put the pencil down and looked at him across the lamp for a while. Then she squared the sheets on the table, knocking their edges together.
“Then you count and I sign,” she said. “I’ve been signing for this line since I was nineteen. I don’t think about it at all.”
“Doesn’t that worry you?”

“No. It’s reed.” She signed the first one while he watched, fast, with her violet-stained fingers, a scrawl like a gull lifting off a post. “There. Nobody died.” She looked past him. “That’s burning.”

It was. They ate it anyway, at the dry end. Lyda said it was cooked, in the tone she used for hulls that would probably make one more run, and ate all of hers and some of his, and told him about a shipmaster on Korinna who had tried to settle his account in dice. Sol read her Teo’s letter. Dear Sol, I am on Berea. It is still evening. Ione Vey says my spelling is a heresy and has started a ledger of it. Tell Lyda I am eating.
“He isn’t,” Lyda said.
Afterward Sol washed the plates, and she sat by the stove checking her own signatures, which made him smile.
“You’re humming,” she said.
“I’m not.”
“Lucan’s written it down.”
“Lucan writes everything down.”
“Then it’s true.”
He listened, and he was. He did not know the tune or where he had got it. For most of his life there had been a hum in his head that was not his. This one was.

When he turned around she was asleep, with the pencil still in her fingers and her head against the wing of the chair. He took the pencil out of her hand. He stood a while looking at her face in the lamplight: forty, and keeping count of it at the corners of the eyes, and between the brows where she frowned at figures. A year a year. He found he could hold that in the same hand as the pencil.

The cup was full. He carried it to the door and emptied it into the yard, into the dark and the rain, and set it back in the pale ring it had worn into the table, where she would know to find it. Then he sat down across from her, and listened to it begin again.

Year ten. Thessa. Tarren, S.: sixty. A crossing now costs him two days’ stiffness; he says one. Seizures this year: four. Thorne, T.: twenty-six. One spell on landing, brief, after which he preached. I notice I have stopped writing down what Tarren says at the meetings. I write down what the boy says. He says it worse, and they remember it.
Thessa had two moons, and one of them was too big.

It hung over the flats by day, pale and enormous, and twice in every long Thessan day it drew the sea out forty kilometers across a plain of grey mud and white salt, and twice it let it come home. It came home faster than anyone could run. The rakers carried horns on cords around their necks, and in the chapel on the shingle ridge above the tideline there was a board of the names of people who had not run fast enough.

The church met in a drying shed that belonged to a widow named Ama Jessop, among racks of salt so dry it cracked the lips. Teo had found them. He had come through on a Thorne run two years before with a night to kill between ships, said the name in a raker’s kitchen, and been asked to say it again. This time he had asked Sol to come with him, and Sol had come, and understood within the first hour that he had been invited the way a son invites his father to see a house he has built.

Teo read to them from his own copy, made over two winters from Lyda’s and spelled as he spelled everything. The Thessans, who had no other, were learning the Gospels with Teo’s spellings and would probably keep them for a hundred years.

They kept turning to Sol. Every question in the shed went past Teo to the old man on the salt sack at the back, where Sol had sat down on the first night because Jory Hask had once put him at the back of a net loft and it had seemed the right place ever since. Bishop? they said. He sent every question back up the room. Teo took them with the expression of a pilot whose instructor will not take his hands off the controls.
On the sixth night a raker named Brann Tolley stood up among the racks. He was a heavy, quiet man with salt in the creases of his knuckles, and he had not spoken before.

“My brother went out for the late rake at the spring tides,” he said. “He was slow on the horn. The chapel relay held him in the holding light for three weeks, and we stood at the Pearl every day and looked at it, and then the relay let him go. The light’s still on. They told us to be calm.” He looked past Teo to the back of the shed. “So where is he?”
Every face turned to Sol.

He had answers, more of them than anyone alive. He had heard the grey static at the gate of heaven in a cellar on Philippa, and knew what it was and what it was not, and none of it was any use to a man who had stood at a Pearl for three weeks. He opened his mouth anyway.
Teo was looking at him. Sol shut his mouth again and kept it shut. It was the hardest silence he had kept in years.

Teo turned back to the raker. “I don’t know where he is,” he said. Then he bent over his copy and turned the pages, too fast, and read, stumbling. “We do not want you to be un... uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.” He stopped, and frowned at the page, and read it again, slowly. Then he looked up. “It doesn’t say don’t grieve. Did you hear that? It says grieve. Only not like it’s the end.”
Brann Tolley stood among the racks with his hands hanging. “So I’m allowed.”
“It’s the first thing it says,” said Teo.

Thessans did not weep easily; the salt dried it out of them, they said. Brann wept. Ama Jessop went and stood beside him with her hand on his back, and after a while two others did, and Teo went on reading, and nobody turned to the back of the shed again that night.
Outside afterward, on the shingle, with the big moon up and the sea coming home across the flats in one long silver line, Teo said, “You didn’t help.”
“No.”
“You were going to.”
“Yes.”
Teo grinned at the sea. “I spelled uninformed wrong. In the copy. They’ve made forty from mine. I’ll have to go round and fix them all.”
He stayed for the tide season. Sol went home on the Linnet with Lucan. Teo came down the hold before they sailed and checked Sol’s pod seal twice.
“I’ve closed a thousand of these,” Teo said.
“Three hundred and six,” said Lucan, from the next pod. “I have the logs.”
The lid came down. The frost came up the glass in its white ferns, and with it, as it always did, the voice, flattened, in his own key. They don’t need you. He doesn’t need you. You’re finished.
“I know,” Sol said to the frost. “Thank God.”
The voice went on a moment, as though it had lost its place. He said the name, and it broke, and he went down into the cold smiling.

Year fifteen. Tarren, S.: sixty-five. Generalized seizure on the Thorne pier, mid-morning, about a minute and fifty, witnessed. Lay down unprompted at the aura. Head cushioned by a child of six, correctly, with her own coat. Post-ictal: confused, then tearful. Asked for cake.
The oranges came at the morning tally, between the ninth bale and the tenth.

He had learned by then. He set the slate down on a bollard and said “Coat” to the nearest person and got himself down onto the boards before the boards could come up to meet him. The nearest person was the cooper’s youngest, who had been on the next bollard watching the cranes. She looked at him with great seriousness and began to unbutton.
Then it was evening, and raining, and he was in the long laboratory.

He knew it at once this time: the tall window streaming, the benches down both sides, the hum in the ceiling lights. Then the lights went out, and someone said Hey, and someone else said Shh, and down the aisle between the benches came a small moving glow. A woman was carrying a cake in both hands, grinning so widely that he could see the gap between her front teeth, and the candlelight was in the gap. Everyone was singing. It was the old song with only one line in it and a name, and they were singing it badly and loudly and on purpose. A tall, heavy man at the next bench could not get up fast enough on his bad knee and sang sitting down, his leg stuck out in the aisle, and the woman stepped over it without looking, as if she had done it a hundred times. A thin young man in a striped scarf, green and orange, conducted with a plastic fork. Somebody’s spectacles, mended with black tape, flashed the flames back. At the end bench a woman with a long nose laughed into a chipped mug with a cat on it before the song was over, and somewhere behind him a laugh he knew, too big for the room.
The name in the song was his. The cake came down in front of him among the cables and the cold coffee, and the light of it was on all their faces, and every one of them was looking at him.
“Make a wish,” somebody said.
He leaned toward the candles and drew a breath, and the light went white.

He came back on the pier under a copper sky, with a small coat folded under his cheek and a small palm resting on the planks an inch from his ear, not touching him. His mouth tasted of his own blood. Every long muscle in him had been worked hard and put away wet. A ring of loaders stood off at a little distance, and nobody had covered anybody’s ears.
The cooper’s girl leaned over him. “A hundred and ten,” she said. “I counted.”
He looked up at her for a long time, trying to remember what he had been about to do.
“Is there any cake?” he said.
She considered it. “No.”

Lyda came down the counting-house stair at a pace that was not quite running. She had stopped running to him years ago, because it frightened the children. She knelt, slowly, and thanked the cooper’s girl as she would have thanked a shipmaster, and gave her back her coat, and sat on the boards with Sol’s head in her lap until he could stand.
That night, in the house across the yard, he told her.

“They sang to me,” he said. “A whole room of them. There was a cake, with candles. I had a birthday, Lyda. Somebody made me a cake.” He turned his hands over on the table. “I can’t find one of their names. Not one. I was about to blow them out.”
She was quiet for a while. The cup was going at the end of the table.
“When was it?”
“I don’t know. It was raining.”
“It’s raining now,” Lyda said. “Then it’s today.”
“What is?”
“Your birthday. You haven’t got one. Now you have.”
“That isn’t how birthdays work.”
“It’s how this one works,” said Lyda. “I keep the books.”
In the morning Lucan wrote it into the record, under the date: Date of birth, previously unknown. Assigned by wife. He underlined wife, and said it was the first reliable figure in the file.

The next year the baker’s wife sent up a cake with the correct number of candles on it, at Lyda’s insistence, and Tobin said it looked like the refinery fires on Plenty. It took Sol three breaths to put them out. Nobody wished him forever. They wished him another one.

That was the spring Wenna Coyle came to a meeting in the warehouse loft. He looked up from the reading and she was there, at the back by the cargo doors, in a good grey coat, with the same smooth face she had worn in Jory’s net loft and two fingers resting at her temple. She stayed through the whole of the reading. Before the prayers she was gone. He did not go after her. He prayed for her that night by name, after Aurelian, and every night after, and she did not come again, and he did not ask anyone what it meant.
Year twenty-two. Lucan, I. Age: sufficient. Objections outstanding: one.

Lyda had taken her objections to Lucan at the end of the pier the year before she went into the river. After it she kept going out there in the evenings, and it was some years before anyone noticed that the questions had changed hands. The doctor brought them now, in a grey book, and drew a line through each when she had answered it to his satisfaction, which was not often. Some had a second line beneath, in her square, impatient hand.

Sol saw the page once, left open on the counting-house table, the spring Lucan turned what Lyda insisted was eighty-three and he insisted was nobody’s business. Every line on it had been struck through but the last.
I would be doing it to please my friends.
And under it, in Lyda’s hand: You have never once in your life done anything to please anybody. L.
A week later there was a line through that one too.

They went down to the Wend at first light, to the place where the bank shelved and the reeds had been trodden into a path. Teo was home that spring, and walked the doctor down the bank with his arm under the old man’s. Lucan took off his spectacles and gave them to Lyda to hold. The Pask girl stood beside her with his bag, as she stood beside him everywhere now; she had come up from Galatia at fifteen with the second box he ever made behind her ear, and stayed to learn how to make the rest. Tobin watched from an upturned crate. Up on the boardwalk, with his slate, Ansel Weir wrote it down.

Sol stood in the cold water to his waist, with the current pulling at his shirt, and Teo brought Lucan out to him. The doctor weighed almost nothing. His eyes without the spectacles looked younger and less certain, and he blinked at Sol as though Sol were a little out of focus.
“Proceed, Tarren,” he said.

Sol put his hand behind the narrow grey head. “In the name of the Father,” he said, “and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Teo took the weight, and they laid him back into the river, and it closed over his face.

He came up gasping. He stood between them in the brown current with the water running out of his hair, and his face did something none of them had ever seen it do. It came apart. He put a hand up to it as if to find out what was happening, and then he wept, standing in the Wend, a very old man with his mouth working and his eyes screwed shut, and looked furious about it.
“I didn’t,” he said. “I hadn’t...” He touched his temple. “It’s stopped. The hum. I haven’t noticed it in fifty years, and I heard it stop.”
On the bank the little church of Philippa had begun to laugh, the way it always did, and Lyda stood among them holding his spectacles in both hands and did not laugh, and did not wipe her face.

Afterward he sat on the bank in a blanket with the ledger on his knees and wrote it down, and Sol, beside him, read it upside down. Immersed, the Wend, first light. Hum ceased. Wept on surfacing; not anticipated. And then, as he had once written it under Sol’s name in a room above a chandlery: Mechanism unknown. He underlined unknown twice.
He sat looking at the page a long time. Then he wrote two more words, and did not underline them.
Cause known.

He lived four years more, which he described as statistically impertinent. He kept the surgery until the chandlery stair beat him, and then gave it to the Pask girl, and in his last autumn he let Lyda move him across the yard into the room where Sol had lived the year before the wedding. He measured Sol for the last time in the first week of the winter, with the calipers shaking in his fingers.
“Seventy-six,” he said, and wrote it down. “You are doing very well, Tarren. For a man of your vintage.”

He died in the chair by the stove in the middle of a winter night, with a book open on his knee and nobody awake. Lyda found him in the morning. She took the spectacles off his face and folded them and put them on the shelf, and no one moved them after.

He had asked Tobin for the stone the autumn before, and Tobin, who was past eighty and slow, had cut it on the pier with the slab across two trestles, a few letters a day, while Lucan came down every afternoon to check the spelling. He had not intended, he said, to be buried under a misprint. It said his name, and Physician, and under that a line Sol knew the source of; Lucan had always said that one of the four accounts read like a case history. Having followed all things closely from the beginning.

They buried him in the field above the dye works, in the rain, and the church of Philippa wept for him openly, and the Pask girl wept loudest. At the graveside it came, flat and catching, in his own voice. Nothing. He’s nothing now. You’ve put him in a hole in the rain. Sol said the name, and the voice went to static. The grief stayed. That was right. That one was his.

Teo had come home for it. When he went out again on the spring run he took the ledgers with him in a sea chest: forty-one of them, bound in grey board, the first one’s spine split and mended with tape, Sol Tarren on its opening page in a small upright hand above everything that came after.

Nobody measured Sol after that. Lyda had no calipers. She had the counting-house stair, nineteen steps with a landing halfway, and she kept count on it the way she kept count of everything that belonged to her line, and for a good many years she managed not to let him see her doing it.

One evening, a long way on, when she had stopped managing it, Sol sat at the table in the house across the yard with the grey notebook open under the lamp. He was reading aloud, because Lyda’s eyes were tired, and she sat across from him with her white head back against the chair and her eyes closed, following the shape of the words. He turned a page, and saw his own hand on it.

It was an old man’s hand. The skin was thin and loose over the knuckles, and on the back of it, among the white hairs, were brown spots, the size of coins. He had seen a hand like it once, in the Bounty Market on Mars, holding a cloth bag against a narrow chest, while a crowd turned its children’s faces away.
He was not afraid of it. He looked at it a long while, and was not afraid.

Outside it had begun to rain, softly, on the roof. Somewhere past the rain and the dark and the long cold between the stars, something still knew to the meter where he sat. It had known for a great many years. It had been patient.
“Sol,” Lyda said, without opening her eyes. “You stopped.”
“I’m here,” he said, and found his place, and read on.
